P10978:
# (salen)Metal-Catalyzed β-Glucuronidation of Alcohols, Phenols, and Anilines

**Authors:** Peyton D. Beyer; Eric N. Jacobsen

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

## Abstract

β-Glucuronidation is an important metabolic pathway for a variety of chemicals including drugs and endogenous substances. We report here that simple (salen)cobalt and (salen)chromium complexes catalyze the β-glucuronidation of alcohols, phenols, and anilines via stereospecific opening of 1,2-anhydroglucuronate electrophiles. The optimized protocol is mild and pH-neutral, enabling β-glucuronidation of complex pharmaceuticals and natural products bearing acid-sensitive and Lewis-basic functionality. Kinetic studies reveal a first-order kinetic dependance on catalyst concentration, which stands in contrast to the (salen)metal -catalyzed opening of simple epoxides where second-order rate dependence on catalyst has been observed consistently.

## Abstract

The development of general laboratory methods for selective glycosylation is a focus of intensive research activity, and recent advances in small-molecule catalysis have greatly expanded synthetic access to challenging glycosidic linkages often with high levels of stereoselectivity and broad functional-group compatibility.1,2 Despite this progress, important limitations remain in chemical glycosylation that could potentially be addressed with the development of new catalytic methods. In that context, β-selective glucuronidation represents an important class of glycosylation reactions where existing methods are often inefficient and lack generality in scope. Glucuronyltransferases are known to target a variety of different protic functional groups present on pharmaceuticals and other bioactive molecules,3–5 but direct isolation of the resulting β-glucuronidated metabolites directly from biological sources is often impractical. Expanded synthetic access to β-glucuronides of medicinally important compounds would facilitate requisite characterization efforts in drug development and could greatly expand the study of these important metabolites (e.g. Figure 1A).6

The preparation of glucoronides by traditional glycosylation methods is rendered challenging by the relatively low reactivity of standard glucuronyl electrophiles, as the electron-withdrawing C6 carboxylic acid group destabilizes buildup of positive charge at the anomeric carbon in the substitution step.7–9 The most common approaches rely on the use of stoichiometric strong Lewis acid activators such as boron trifluoride and reliance on neighboring-group participation with 2-O-ester-protected glucuronyl electrophiles to control stereoselectivity (Figure 1B).10–13 This approach often also results in the formation of orthoester and transesterification side products resulting from direct nucleophilic attack at the oxocarbenium carbon of the bridged intermediate (Figure 1B, bottom). While sterically hindered esters can be employed to suppress side product formation,14 their subsequent deprotection in turn requires strong base and extended reaction times, leading to decomposition via E1cb pathways.15 In addition, the use of strong Lewis acids introduces potential incompatibilities with Lewis-basic functional groups common in pharmaceuticals.16,17 While milder biocatalytic approaches have been explored, current methods tend to suffer from relatively limited nucleophile scope, poor yields, high cost of the requisite UDP-glucuronic acid donor, and low solution stability of glucuronyltransferase enzymes.18–23

We sought to develop a small-molecule-catalyzed mild and general approach to stereoselective glucuronidation that might overcome the reactivity and selectivity challenges associated with the use of strong Lewis acids and 2-O-ester-mediated stereochemical control. Our group has previously employed precisely designed bis-thiourea catalysts to promote stereospecific β-glycosylations of a wide variety of glycosyl electrophiles.24–29 However, in our hands thiourea catalysis has proven entirely unsuccessful for glucuronidation reactions, a likely direct result of the intrinsically low reactivity of glucuronyl donors. In considering alternative approaches, we were drawn to the pioneering research by Danishefsky and Gin that applied epoxy glycals (1,2-anhydropyranosides) as glycosyl donors.28–30 Given the extensive applications of (salen)metal catalysts in stereoselective opening of epoxides,33–35 we considered whether 1,2-anhydro derivatives of glucuronides might be suitable substrates for stereospecific epoxide opening. Herein, we report a general and functional-group-tolerant catalytic platform for β-glucuronidation, in which simple, achiral (salen)metal complexes promote the stereospecific opening of 1,2-anhydroglucuronate electrophiles with alcohols, phenols, and anilines (Figure 1C). We demonstrate the versatility of this platform in the glucuronidation of a diverse set of pharmaceuticals and natural products, highlighting the potentially broad utility of this method for metabolite synthesis.

The requisite 1,2-anhydro glucuronate electrophiles 3 (Figure 2) were accessed efficiently from the precursor glucuronal via highly diastereoselective (>20:1 d.r.) Shi epoxidation.36,37 The methyl or benzyl esters (3a or 3b) were used interchangeably in the catalytic glycosylation reactions with very similar results.38 With functional group compatibility and breadth of scope as foremost considerations, we focused our catalyst development efforts around four distinct model nucleophiles, alcohols Boc-Ser-OMe (4a) and fluphenazine (4b), phenol Boc-Tyr-OMe (5a), and aniline para-toluidine (6a). Catalyst structure and reaction conditions were optimized to maximize the yield of the β-glucuronidation product while minimizing hydrolysis and polymerization, which are typical competing pathways in ring-opening glycosylations.38,39

Salen complexes of cobalt(III) and chromium(III) bearing sulfonate axial ligands40,41 proved to be effective in promoting all three model reactions (Figure 1). Stereochemistry in the salen ligand was found to have no impact on reaction outcomes, and achiral ethylene diamine-derived catalysts 1 and 2 were identified as optimal. The only additional catalyst parameters that were found to require specific matching to the nucleophile of interest were thus the identity of the metal and the sulfonate counterion, and the para-substituents on the salen ligand. In all successful reactions, complete stereoinversion in the ring-opening glucuronidations was observed, with only the β-glucuronide observed along with trace amounts of the α-mannouronide deriving from the β-epoxide impurity in 3.29,42

A selection of results generated from the optimization studies for glucuronidation of 4a and 4b is provided in Figure 2A. For these model substrates, the Co and Cr complexes 1 and 2 generally performed similarly. A broad survey (Fig. S12) of Lewis acids precedented to be effective in promoting glycosylation reactions and/or nucleophilic opening of epoxides was performed with 4b, with only InBr3 found to promote glucuronidation in appreciable (28%) yield (Fig. 2A, entry 8). The (salen)Co(OMs) 1b complex exhibited higher activity at lower concentrations and was identified as optimal (Figure S14). Use of excess electrophile 3 resulted in increased product yields and reaction rate and allowed use of lower catalyst loadings (entries 9–10). Thus the optimized conditions were ultimately determined to be 5 mol% of (salen)Co(OMs) 1a with 3 equivalents of 2b in dichloromethane solvent at 2 M concentration in the presence of 3 Å molecular sieves as a desiccant. Glucuronide 3a was thus obtained in 83% yield (determined by NMR) with full conversion of 2b. Unproductive pathways responsible for the decomposition of 3 were determined to consist primarily of hydrolysis and oligomerization reactions.

In the attempted glucuronidation of phenol 5a, only trace formation of the desired glucuronidation product 8a was observed (Fig. 2B, entry 1). The alcohol product (or its precursor alkoxide) is more reactive toward 3 than the phenolic substrate, resulting in complete consumption of the epoxide and formation of oligomeric products. Addition of 1 equiv. of diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA) was found to inhibit glucuronidation of alcohols such as 4a but not of phenol 5a. Thus, inclusion of DIPEA was found to prevent oligomerization from outcompeting phenol glucuronidation in the reaction of 5a and favor formation of the desired product 8a. No product formation was observed with DIPEA in the absence of (salen)metal catalyst (entry 5). Significantly improved reaction rates were obtained with (salen)Cr complexes compared to the cobalt analogues (entries 2–3), with the best results obtained with catalyst 2c bearing the less sterically hindered ligand (entry 4). The catalyst optimization directed toward glucuronidation of aniline 6a revealed a relatively flat landscape (Figure 2C), with (salen)Cr(OMs) complex 2b identified as a moderately effective promoter of the desired transformation (entry 3).

Having identified a set of optimized conditions with the different model substrates, the generality of the method was assessed with a variety of densely functionalized pharmaceuticals and natural products. A variety of primary and secondary alcohols were found to be effective substrates for the glucuronidation method using (salen)Co complex 1b (Figure 3A). Excellent tolerance was observed for Lewis basic functionality including amides (4a, 4e, 4g), basic aromatic heterocycles (4c-d), and tertiary amines (4b, 4e). Site-selectivity was observed with substrates bearing multiple hydroxyl groups, with glucuronidation occurring exclusively at the less hindered positions (4f-g). The mildness of the reaction conditions allowed for glucuronidation of substates as functionally rich as paclitaxel 4g. Substrates bearing electron-rich aromatic heterocycles, such as 4c, required higher catalyst loadings to proceed at a useful rate, likely due to competitive unproductive catalyst binding. However, alcohols bearing unhindered and electron-rich Lewis basic heterocycles were found to be completely unreactive and therefore represent a limitation to this method (Figure S15).

Successful phenolic substrates included those possessing functionality such as amides, including β-lactams (5a-5b, 5d), tertiary amines (5c, 5e), basic aromatic heterocycles (5d-e), and sulfides (5d). Ezetimibe 5b, which possesses both a phenol and a secondary alcohol, underwent reaction with complete chemoselectivity for the phenol, enabling the direct synthesis of the natural metabolite. The reaction was also found to be tolerant to a degree of steric hinderance around the phenol. For instance, ortho-substituted phenol 5c was found to undergo glucuronidation in similar yield to that obtained with less hindered phenols. In contrast, the ortho-alkyl-substituted 5e, underwent reaction at a significantly slower rate.

The glucuronidation method is also illustrated with three aniline-containing pharmaceuticals (Figure 3C). It was observed during optimization that smaller excess of epoxide (1.25–2.25 equiv. compared to 3.00 equiv. for alcohols and phenols) was necessary to avoid formation of multiply glucuronidated products. As with alcohol and phenol substrates, the catalytic reaction tolerated the presence of Lewis-basic groups such as various basic aromatic heterocycles (6b-d) and a phosphonamidate (6c). Sulfamethoxazole 6b, which is metabolized in nature by glucuronidation at the sulfonamide, was found to undergo reaction at the aniline nitrogen. Even electron-poor aminopurine and aminopyrimidine substrates 6c-d displayed useful levels of reactivity under the catalytic protocol.

Previous kinetic analyses of (salen)metal-catalyzed ring-opening of meso or terminal epoxides with azide, water, phenols, and primary alcohols as nucleophiles have consistently revealed second-order kinetic dependence on the metal catalyst.40,43–45 These observations are consistent with a mechanism involving independent activation of both nucleophile and epoxide by two different metal complexes, and rate-determining ring opening in a cooperative, bimetallic mechanism. Those insights ultimately guided the design of multimeric complexes with dramatically enhanced reactivity.44 We questioned whether a similar cooperative mechanism was operative in the reactions of epoxide 3, particularly since multimeric catalysts were found to perform no better than the monomeric analogues (Figure S3). Experiments were therefore undertaken to determine the kinetic order in catalyst in the glucuronidation reaction. We selected 1-octanol as the nucleophile since it undergoes clean glucuronidation with 3b in the presence of catalyst 2b with no detectable oligomerization. Reactions were monitored at varying catalyst loadings and the data analyzed using the method developed by Burés (Figure 4).46 The overlays in the time-adjusted concentration plots are distinctly better for a first-order kinetic fit, consistent with a mono metallic mechanism. The (salen)metal complex is thus proposed to operate solely as a Lewis acid to provide mild activation of the 1,2-anhydro pyranoside in the nucleophilic addition while avoiding spontaneous decomposition of the electrophile and inhibition by Lewis-basic functionality.

In summary, we have demonstrated a general approach to β-glucuronidation of alcohols, phenols and anilines under mild, pH-neutral, and nucleophile-limiting conditions using simple, achiral (salen)metal catalysis. This method will hopefully broaden the scope of bioactive compounds of interest that may be subjected to direct chemical glucuronidation and thereby prove enabling in the study of drug metabolites and potential beneficial effects of glucuronidation on drug properties. Current efforts are directed towards the exploration of other classes of ring-opening glycosylation amenable to catalysis by (salen)metal complexes.

# β-Selective 2-Deoxy- and 2,6-Dideoxyglucosylations Catalyzed by Bis-Thioureas

**Authors:** Peyton D. Beyer; Michael M. Nielsen; Elias Picazo; Eric N. Jacobsen

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, United States

## Abstract

We present methods for β-selective 2-deoxy and 2,6-dideoxyglucosylations of natural products, carbohydrates, and amino acids using bis-thiourea hydrogen-bond-donor catalysts. Disarming ester protecting groups were necessary to counter the high reactivity of 2-deoxyglycosyl electrophiles toward non-stereospecific SN1 pathways. Alcohol and phenol nucleophiles with both base- and acid-sensitive functionalities were compatible with the catalytic protocol, enabling access to a wide array of 2-deoxy-β-O-glucosides.

## Abstract

β-Configured 2-deoxy glycosides are integral components in various biologically active natural products (Figure 1A).1,2 The most conceptually straightforward approach to the synthesis of β−2-deoxyglycosides involves stereospecific invertive displacement of appropriate and often readily available α-configured glycosyl electrophiles. However, these electrophiles are highly prone to inherently α-selective non-stereospecific SN1-like pathways due to the electron-rich nature of the site of nucleophilic substitution relative to fully oxygenated analogs (Figure 1B).3–7

As such, application of otherwise β-selective glycosylation protocols to 2-deoxyglycosylations has proven challenging,8–10 and the synthesis of 2-deoxy-β-glycosides has remained a long-standing challenge in the field.11 The Bennett group devised a strategy of in situ generation of α-glycosyl sulfonates and stereospecific displacement by strongly nucleophilic potassium alkoxides, allowing the synthesis of β-linked 2-deoxyoligosaccharides and 2-deoxyglycoside natural products.12–17 However, the need for strongly basic conditions limited its application with base-sensitive functionalities. Li and coworkers developed a directing-group strategy with trimethylsilyl trifluoromethanesulfonate catalysis.18,19 Excellent β-selectivities were obtained, but the requirement for a strongly Lewis acidic catalyst renders the method incompatible with Lewis-basic functionalities. An alternative strategy, reported by Niu and coworkers, employs palladium catalysis to achieve stereo- and chemoselective 2-deoxy glycosylations of phenols across a remarkable scope of nucleophiles and electrophiles.20 This notable advance in functional-group-compatible 2-deoxy glycosylations notwithstanding, a mild and general protocol for the 2-deoxy-β-glycosylation of both phenols and alcohols remains elusive. Other methods, including umpolung strategies,21–24 C-2 auxiliaries,25–28 boronic acid catalysis,29 supramolecular capsules,30 gold-catalyzed activation of alkynyl naphtoates,31 and acid-catalyzed substitutions at cryogenic temperatures,32–35 similarly lack generality in nucleophile scope or require multi-step protocols.

Our group previously developed stereospecific β-glycosylations with glycosyl phosphates promoted by bis-thiourea hydrogen-bond-donor (HBD) catalysts.36–39 Extensive experimental and computational evidence has been advanced consistent with a mechanism of substitution involving dual activation of both the electrophile and nucleophile via general acid/base interactions (Figure 1C). Precise geometrical preorganization and matching of the hydrogen-bond-donating and -accepting domains of the catalysts were critical for achieving high levels of stereospecificity. Here, we report the successful extension of this dual activation strategy to β-selective 2-deoxy- and 2,6-dideoxyglucosylations of amino acids, carbohydrates, natural products, and pharmaceuticals. The approach relies on precise tuning of the bis-thiourea catalysts together with utilization of precisely tuned phosphate leaving groups and disarming protecting groups40,41 to attenuate the inherent reactivity of the deoxy- and dideoxy-glucosyl electrophiles.

Our initial studies found that glycosylations with armed40,41 2-deoxyglucosyl chlorides yielded promising results with highly nucleophilic primary and secondary alcohols.42 However, subsequent efforts to effect glycosylation of complex nucleophiles with 2-deoxyglycosyl chlorides proved unsuccessful, as we observed significant elimination to the glucals and found that the HCl byproduct generated could not be trapped efficiently enough to avoid substrate decomposition via Ferrier rearrangements.43,44 Given the especially successful application of glycosyl phosphates in stereospecific glycosylations promoted by bis-thioureas, we refocused our efforts towards identifying 2-deoxy glucosyl phosphate derivatives with the appropriate balance of stability and reactivity properties.36–39 Glucosyl phosphates bearing electron-rich arming40,41 protecting groups such as benzyl ethers were found to undergo immediate decomposition during attempted preparation and/or isolation. Even disarmed 2-deoxyglucose derivatives bearing carboxylate protecting groups proved too unstable in the case of diaryl phosphate derivatives. However, analogous dialkyl phosphate derivatives were synthesized by reacting the corresponding thioglucosides with N-iodosuccinimide and the desired dialkylphosphate45 and found to be bench-stable and readily purified. Evaluation of this class of electrophiles in the 2-deoxyglucosylation of threonine derivative 3a led to identification of glucosyl phosphate 2a as displaying the most promising levels of reactivity and selectivity for formation of the β-glucoside product. Extensive evaluation of reaction conditions revealed the optimal solvent, concentration, temperature, and reaction time for the model 2-deoxyglucosylation of 3a and molecular sieves as a crucial additive to sequester the phosphoric acid leaving group and minimize electrophile hydrolysis (see Supporting Information for details).36–39 Catalyst optimization efforts included extensive variation of the pyrrolidine substituents, as these components had proven to be crucial handles for tuning reactivity and selectivity in previous glycosylation studies.36,38 In the case of the model 2-deoxyglucosylation reaction, bis-thiourea derivative 1a, which bears an electron-rich 5-N-methyl indolyl substituent in the “northern” fragment and an unsubstituted pyrrolidine in the “southern” fragment, was found to be the most effective with respect to both β-selectivity and yield, the latter feature resulting from minimization of glucal side-product formation arising from elimination.

The scope of suitable nucleophilic partners in 2-deoxy-β-glucosylation reactions with electrophile 2a promoted with catalyst 1a was explored (Figure 2). Focus was placed on couplings where mild conditions would be advantageous compared to existing protocols that rely on either stoichiometric metal amide base or catalytic strong Lewis acids. Reactions were performed with two equivalents of 2a to compensate for unproductive consumption of electrophile through elimination and hydrolysis pathways. Alcohols bearing base-sensitive functional groups, such as protected amino acids (3a-3b) or pleuromutilin (3e), which possesses an enolizable stereocenter, underwent reaction with high β-selectivity without erosion of stereopurity. Deoxy-sugar-based acceptors (3c and 3d) were excellent substrates, yielding disaccharides with high selectivity and efficiency. Alcohols with acid-sensitive functionalities, including hemiacetals (3f and 3j), tertiary amines (3g and 3i), and aromatic heterocycles (3h), also underwent 2-deoxyglucosylation by the catalytic approach. Basic alumina was required for substrates with basic-nitrogen functionality (3g-3h, 3m) to prevent the formation of ammonium phosphate salts, which inhibit thiourea catalysts. The particularly challenging alcohols 3h-3j possessing both base- and acid-sensitive functionality were also found to be suitable substrates under the catalytic conditions.

Phenolic nucleophiles were also demonstrated to be useful partners in the catalytic couplings, albeit under a slightly modified reaction protocol. Increased dilution relative to the glucosylation of alcohols ([4]0 = 0.025 M vs. [3]0 = 0.2 M), and addition of basic alumina were found to enhance β-selectivity (Figures S9, S12). Phenols bearing functionality such as amides (4a) and indoles (4b) proved to be effective coupling partners. In addition, tertiary-amine-containing (4c) and sterically hindered (4d) phenols underwent 2-deoxyglucosylation with good levels of β-selectivity, albeit in modest yields. Finally, glucosylation of β-estradiol 4e was observed to occur with moderate selectivity for the phenolic position.

We then investigated whether principles used in 2-deoxy-β-glucosylations could be applied to the more challenging 2,6-dideoxy-β-glucosylations. Disarmed diacetoxy-substituted derivatives were too unstable for isolation and application in the catalytic reaction, so we evaluated a series of 2,6-dideoxy-L-glucose derivatives with various protecting group schemes and phosphate leaving groups. Bis-trichloroacetyl (TCA) derivative 7a was identified as displaying the best compromise between reactivity and stability. Threonine derivative 3a displayed poor reactivity as a nucleophile, so tyrosine derivative 4a was used as the model substrate in catalyst optimization studies to enable accurate determination of α/β-selectivities by 1H-NMR analysis of crude reaction mixtures. In a survey of bis-thioureas with different arylpyrrolidine substituents, the 2-naphthyl substituted ent-1b, previously effective in site-selective glycosylations,39 provided the best yields and β-selectivity (Figures S14-S15). As observed in prior studies, the absolute stereochemistry of the catalyst influenced reaction outcomes (Figure S16A).).36–38 ent-1 catalysts induced improved yield and β-selectivity with 2,6-dideoxy-L-glucose derivatives (7), whereas the enantiomeric 1 catalysts were more effective with the pseudo-enantiomeric 2-deoxy-D-glucose derivatives (2).

The scope of nucleophiles in 2,6-dideoxyglucosylation reactions is shown in Figure 3. It was observed that unavoidable yield losses attributable to partial loss of the TCA protecting groups were occurring during product isolation, so a quantitative deprotection procedure was developed, isolating products as unprotected 2,6-dideoxy-glucosides (8 or 9). Alcohols and phenols generally reacted with moderate β-selectivity, including functionally rich amino acids (3a-b, 4a), natural products (3e, 4e-4g), and synthetic pharmaceuticals (3h, 3d). β-Estradiol (4e) reacted with modest chemoselectivity for the phenol, yielding the phenolic glucoside with good β-selectivity. The N-heterocycle-containing substrate 3h was glucosylated in good yield, however substrates with strongly basic and nucleophilic amines were incompatible with the 2,6-dideoxyglucosylation protocol, unlike in 2-deoxyglucosylations.

Previous studies on glycosylation reactions of fully oxygenated α-glycosyl donors promoted by bis-thiourea HBD catalysts have provided evidence that β-selectivity arises from predominant stereoinvertive substitution at the anomeric position.36–39,42 However, and as noted above, 2-deoxyglycosyl donors are far more prone to undergo epimerization or substitution via SN1 pathways (Figure 1B). To probe the origin of β-selectivity in 2-deoxyglucosylations promoted by 1a, compound 2a was prepared in two different levels of anomeric purity (α:β = >20:1 and 3.3:1) and subjected to the optimized reaction conditions for glucosylation of 3a and 4a. Very similar β-selectivities were observed regardless of the anomeric purity of 2a (Figure 4A). These results are consistent with product distribution governed by either Curtin-Hammett control over rapidly equilibrating anomers of 2a, stereospecific reaction via a single anomer of 2a, or stereoselective nucleophilic substitution through a common reactive intermediate. To distinguish these two scenarios, the glycosylation of 3b with different anomeric mixtures of 2a (α:β = >20:1 and 2.5:1) was halted at low conversion and the anomeric composition of unconsumed 2a in each reaction was determined (Figure 4B). The observed lack of convergence in the anomeric ratio of 2a, despite a significant degree of product formation, is inconsistent with the rapid equilibration reflective of Curtin-Hammett control. In contrast to the findings depicted in Figure 4A, an analogous set of experiments with the 2,6-dideoxyglucosyl phosphate revealed different levels of β-selectivity are obtained using 2b with different initial levels of anomeric purity (Figure 2C). Thus, the two different classes of deoxyglucosyl phosphates appear to undergo substitution with different levels of stereospecificity.

Heterogenous additives play a critical role in the deoxyglucosylation reactions described above. As in previously studied HBD-catalyzed glycosylations with glycosyl phosphates,36–39 added 4Å molecular sieves are required to sequester the phosphoric acid byproduct formed during the glycosylation. Our present study has further shown that use of basic alumina improves the β-selectivity of phenolic 2-deoxyglucosylations. In the absence of both 4Å molecular sieves and basic alumina, α-enriched 2,6-dideoxyglucosyl phosphate 7a was observed by NMR to undergo anomerization to approximately 6:1 α:β mixtures, followed by rapid decomposition (Figure 4D). Anomerization was not observed in the presence of 4Å molecular sieves, indicating that small amounts of phosphoric acid likely promotes the anomerization process. In addition, the combination of basic alumina and 4Å molecular sieves was found to improve the efficiency of sequestering soluble phosphoric acid (Figure S24). We propose that such efficient sequestration is needed for reaching optimal levels of β-selectivity in phenolic glucosylations by suppressing both undesired, phosphoric acid-catalyzed background reactions as well as in situ anomerization to β-phosphates. However, low concentrations of soluble phosphoric acid do not appear to have the same deleterious effect on glucosylations of alcohols.

In summary, we have developed catalytic and β-selective 2-deoxy and 2,6-dideoxyglucosylations, providing a viable new approach to these longstanding challenges in glycosylation chemistry. The versatility of these methods is demonstrated by the successful synthesis of 2-deoxyglucosides with various nucleophiles featuring both acid- and base-sensitive functionalities. Successful glucosylations with both 2-deoxy and 2,6-dideoxysugars necessitated specific modifications to electrophiles and catalysts. Together with the observation of different degrees of stereospecificity between these two systems, our results underscore the challenges of stereoselective glycosylations with deoxy sugars. We are hopeful that the strategies applied in this work will help spur further advances in selective glycosylation with different classes of deoxysugars.
